    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
src/main/resources/application.yaml (comments abridged)
spring:
  application:
    name: acp-meridian              # also names ~/.config/acp-meridian/ for the MCP sign-ins
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        runtime: goose                  # the only line that picks the agent
        workspace: ${WORKSPACE_DIR:./workspace}   # AGENTS.md lives here

        model: deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731
        provider:                       # a platform's OpenAI-compatible endpoint
          id: openai
          api-type: openai
          base-url: ${GENAI_API_BASE}
          api-key: ${GENAI_API_KEY}
        on-unsupported: warn

        mcp-servers:                    # each user signs in; the agent never sees a token
          - name: finops-mcp
            url: https://mcp-gateway.example.com/finops-mcp/mcp
            auth: oauth
          - name: servicedesk-mcp
            url: https://mcp-gateway.example.com/servicedesk-mcp/mcp
            auth: oauth
        mcp:
          oauth:
            mode: local                 # terminal app: browser sign-in, tokens in a mode-600 file
            client-name: Meridian Capacity & Cost Agent

        skills:                         # fetched into workspace/.agents/skills before the agent starts
          - url: https://github.com/cpage-pivotal/claude-plugin-marketplace
            path: plugins/mailgun/skills/mailgun

        runtimes:                       # read only by the runtime it names
          goose:
            mcp:
              answer-discover: true     # this gateway breaks goose's discovery probe

        permissions:
          policy: auto-approve          # the real gate is in AGENTS.md: confirm before createTicket
        console:                        # spring-ai-acp-harness-client-console
          title: Meridian Logistics — Capacity & Cost Agent
          greeting: Ask about your capacity and cost findings, or what they are costing you.
          session: meridian-console
        filesystem:
          enabled: false
        terminal:
          enabled: false
        timeout: 5m
        pool:
          max-processes: 1
          max-sessions-per-process: 4
          session-ttl: 60m

  main:
    web-application-type: none

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
The system prompt is workspace/AGENTS.md, checked in next to the code. It defines the audience, lists the MCP tools and which of them need the user's explicit confirmation, and lays out the workflow. An excerpt:

workspace/AGENTS.md (excerpt)
# Meridian Logistics Capacity & Cost Agent

You help **business unit staff at Meridian Logistics** understand capacity and cost
issues flagged against their workloads on the shared private cloud, and file service
desk requests to get them fixed.

## Available Tools

**FinOps Insights**: read-only, no side effects, call freely:
- `getBusinessUnitSummary()`: the caller's business unit: budget, spend, forecast
- `listFindings(severity?, status?)`: flagged capacity/cost issues

**Service Desk**:

*Requires explicit human confirmation:*
- `createTicket(requestType, fields)`: files a real request that real people will act on

docs.title: The code
docs.text:
One class, and it names neither an agent nor a UI:

MeridianApplication.java
@SpringBootApplication
public class MeridianApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(MeridianApplication.class, args);
    }
}

The read-prompt-stream loop, the rendering of tool calls and plans, Ctrl-C cancellation and the session commands all come from spring-ai-acp-harness-client-console. Before that module existed, this application carried two classes of its own for it, which is what prompted the module.

docs.title: Running it on each runtime
docs.text:
set -a && source .envrc && set +a
mvn package

java -jar target/acp-meridian-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar                              # goose
java -jar target/acp-meridian-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar --spring.ai.acp.harness.runtime=opencode   # same endpoint, same result
java -jar target/acp-meridian-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar --spring.profiles.active=codex  # OpenAI itself

Goose and OpenCode reach the platform's Chat Completions endpoint unchanged. Codex speaks only the Responses API, which that endpoint does not serve, so a codex profile swaps model and provider for OpenAI:

application.yaml (continued)
---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: codex
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        runtime: codex
        model: gpt-5.6-terra
        provider:
          id: openai
          api-type: openai
          base-url: ""                  # clear the platform endpoint
          api-key: ${OPENAI_API_KEY}    # reaches Codex via ACP authenticate; never written to disk

MCP servers, sign-in, skill and AGENTS.md are identical on all three.

docs.title: Testing your application
docs.text:
Switch the auto-configuration off and mock the client. No agent process, no provider key:

@SpringBootTest(properties = "spring.ai.acp.harness.enabled=false")
class ReviewControllerTests {

    @MockitoBean
    AcpHarnessClient acpHarnessClient;

    @Test
    void summarizes() {
        AcpHarnessClient.PromptSpec spec = mock(AcpHarnessClient.PromptSpec.class, RETURNS_SELF);
        AcpHarnessClient.AcpHarnessResponse response = mock(AcpHarnessClient.AcpHarnessResponse.class);
        given(acpHarnessClient.prompt()).willReturn(spec);
        given(acpHarnessClient.prompt(anyString())).willReturn(spec);   // prompt(text) is a default method
        given(spec.call()).willReturn(response);
        given(response.content()).willReturn("Looks good");
        // …
    }
}

For a test against a real agent, gate it on the agent being usable so CI without one stays green, and pin the model so a developer's local agent config cannot change the outcome.

docs.title: Testing a runtime adapter
docs.text: spring-ai-acp-harness-client-test is for adapter authors. AcpHarnessRuntimeContract is the conformance suite every compiled adapter extends; it asserts only what ACP standardizes. ScriptedAcpAgent is a fake agent speaking raw JSON-RPC over an in-memory transport, and AcpHarnessProbe skips live suites when an agent is absent or has no credentials. Live suites cost real tokens, so they only run with -Dspring-ai-acp-harness-client.test.live=true.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix Startup fails: spring.ai.acp.harness.runtime is not set and more than one runtime adapter is on the classpath Set spring.ai.acp.harness.runtime to one of the listed ids. Startup fails: No AcpHarnessRuntime registered for spring.ai.acp.harness.runtime='…' Add that runtime's starter, or spring-ai-acp-harness-client-boot-starter-registry for a registry id. Startup fails: spring.ai.acp.harness.runtimes has options for unregistered runtime(s) A tier-3 block names a runtime nothing supplies; usually a typo. workspace '…' is not an existing directory Create it first; Spring AI ACP Harness Client will not. A relative path is resolved against the JVM's working directory. The first prompt fails with Could not install skill … A skill failed to fetch or check. Pin a ref that exists, check path, make sure git is installed, and remove any symlinks from the skill. The agent ignores AGENTS.md It is not at the root of the workspace actually used; check the workspace in the startup INFO line. A skill is never used Check <workspace>/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md exists, the description says when to use it, and the agent has the tools it needs (goose: builtins: developer). The model says it has no tools from an MCP server The server failed to load, which ACP never reports. On goose, check the notices() or WARN log; try mcp.answer-discover for gateways; confirm HTTPS, headers and OAuth sign-in. Tool calls are refused Default policy: deny. Use allowlist with names read off a DEBUG log, or auto-approve. A warning that a model or mode cannot be honoured The agent does not advertise the value; the warning lists what it does offer. With your own endpoint, check its /models. Codex: Authentication required No usable login: set spring.ai.acp.harness.provider.api-key (and api-type: openai). Against your own endpoint, check it serves the Responses API. Goose cannot find the key goose configure saved The adapter sets GOOSE_DISABLE_KEYRING=1, so a key kept in the OS keychain is not read. Set spring.ai.acp.harness.provider.api-key, or export the provider's key variable. Turns end in Failed with a timeout Raise spring.ai.acp.harness.timeout, or per turn with .options(o -> o.timeout(…)).

docs.title: Terminal Console
docs.text:
spring-ai-acp-harness-client-console turns the application into a terminal chat with its agent. It is for the stage where you are designing the agent itself — its AGENTS.md, its skills, its MCP servers — and want to talk to it before there is any other front end. Add the dependency and run the application; there is no code to write.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-acp-harness-client-console</artifactId>
    <version>${spring-ai-acp-harness-client.version}</version>
</dependency>

It opens the session before the first prompt, so the model the negotiated tier actually applied is on screen before any tokens are spent, along with anything the agent reported outside the protocol, such as an MCP server it could not load. Each turn is streamed: assistant text as it arrives, a dimmed line per tool call, thought and plan update, a line for any tool call that fails, and the agent's context usage when the turn ends.

Meridian Logistics — Capacity & Cost Agent
runtime: opencode   ·   /help for commands, /exit to quit
  MODEL: deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 → acp/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 (CONFIG_OPTION)

Ask about your capacity and cost findings, or what they are costing you.

you › what are my open findings costing me?
  → getBusinessUnitSummary
  → listFindings
(the answer streams in here as the agent writes it)

docs.title: When it runs
docs.text:
The module is safe to leave on the classpath of an application that is also tested and deployed, because by default the console only starts when the process is attached to an interactive terminal. Nothing is registered otherwise: no bean, no terminal, and nothing reading stdin.

spring.ai.acp.harness.console.enabled Behaviour unset (default) Runs when stdin and stdout are a terminal: java -jar or mvn spring-boot:run from a shell. A test, a CI job or a deployed service is left alone. true Always runs, reading plain lines when there is no terminal. For driving it from a pipe or a script. false Never runs.

The console starts on its own thread once the application is ready, so startup completes normally and a web application keeps serving while it runs. When the user leaves, the console closes the application context, which stops the agent and ends the process. In a web application that stops the server too.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
Input Effect Any text A turn in the current named session, so the agent remembers earlier turns. Line editing and history (kept across runs) come from JLine; a multi-line paste is one prompt. Ctrl-C during a turn Cancels the turn (the client sends session/cancel) and returns to the prompt with the conversation intact. Ctrl-C at the prompt Clears the line. /exit, /quit, Ctrl-D Leaves. /new Starts a fresh conversation in a new named session, closing the old one where the agent supports session/close. /sessions Lists the conversations the agent has stored, marking the current one. Needs session/list. /resume <id> Continues a stored conversation, with session/resume or else session/load. /notices Everything the agent has reported outside the protocol (see When a server fails to load). /help Lists the commands. Tab completes them.

When the agent does not implement a session operation, the command says which ACP method is missing rather than failing.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: Property Default Description spring.ai.acp.harness.console.enabled unset See When it runs. spring.ai.acp.harness.console.title spring.application.name The heading shown at startup. spring.ai.acp.harness.console.greeting none Shown once before the first prompt, to tell the user what to ask. spring.ai.acp.harness.console.session console The named session turns run in. /new and /resume move to <session>-1, -2, and so on. spring.ai.acp.harness.console.history-file ~/.config/<spring.application.name>/console-history Input history, kept across runs. Honours $XDG_CONFIG_HOME, like the MCP sign-in file. Not written when input is piped. spring.ai.acp.harness.console.show-thoughts true Show the reasoning the agent surfaces, one dimmed line per thought.

docs.title: Answering permission requests
docs.text:
With policy: ask, the console puts each of the agent's permission requests to you, part-way through the turn, as a numbered choice between the options the agent offered:

spring:
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        mode: plan              # so the agent asks before it acts (see "Mode decides whether the question is asked")
        permissions:
          policy: ask

  ? The agent wants to: Run `./send-report.sh`  (execute · developer__shell)
    1) Allow once
    2) Always allow
    3) Reject
  choose 1-3 (Ctrl-C to cancel) › 3

Ctrl-C at that prompt cancels the request, which the agent hears as a cancellation rather than a refusal. A question still open when its turn ends, because it exceeded timeout, is taken down and answered the same way. This is the most direct way to see what an agent is about to do while designing it. It is also a prompt per tool call, so an agent whose job is calling tools may be better served by allowlist and a gate in its instructions, as acp-meridian does.

Note

Time spent answering counts against the turn's spring.ai.acp.harness.timeout. The prompt applies to every session in the application, not only the console's, so an application that also serves web users should leave ask to the console-only profile it runs locally.

docs.title: Customizing
docs.text:
• How turns look: register a subclass of ConsoleRenderer as a bean. Every method is an override point, and render(AcpHarnessEvent) is the one each event goes through.
  • Who answers ask: register your own PermissionPrompt bean, and the console's backs off. PermissionQuestion carries the tool name, the agent's title for the call, its kind and the options.
  • The terminal: a JLine Terminal bean replaces the system one.

Tip

Log lines are written to the same terminal and land in the middle of the conversation. A console application usually wants logging.level.root: WARN and a bare pattern such as logging.pattern.console: "%msg%n", as acp-meridian uses.

docs.title: HTTP Endpoint
docs.text:
An optional WebFlux controller exposes the agent over HTTP. It requires spring-boot-starter-webflux and spring.ai.acp.harness.controller.enabled=true, so adding either alone publishes nothing.

spring:
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        controller:
          enabled: true
          path: /api/acp
          allow-unauthenticated: false    # requests need a Principal
          allow-request-overrides: false  # a request may not choose its own model or provider
          max-prompt-chars: 32000
          max-timeout: 10m
Endpoint Behaviour POST {path}/prompt Body {"prompt", "session", "timeout", "model", "provider", "mode"}; returns {"content", "stopReason", "error", "requestId"}. POST {path}/stream Same body; server-sent events of assistant text only (tool calls and plans can name workspace paths). GET {path}/sessions The caller's open sessions, sorted by name: [{"name", "sessionId", "title", "updatedAt"}]. name is the name the caller gave, which continues or closes the session. title and updatedAt come from the agent and are null when it does not implement session/list. DELETE {path}/sessions/{name} Closes one of the caller's named sessions. Returns 204 whether or not the name was in use. GET {path}/health Unauthenticated; whether the agent is up, and which runtime.

docs.title: Sessions belong to the caller
docs.text:
The session name in a request is scoped to whoever sent it, so two users choosing the same name get separate conversations, and neither can see, continue or close the other's. Without a Principal, as with allow-unauthenticated, all callers share one scope.

Names follow the usual session name rules, up to 109 characters; anything else is a 400. The scope means the endpoint cannot reach a session your application opened itself through AcpHarnessClient under the same name. GET {path}/sessions lists only sessions open in this process, so it does not include stored sessions from earlier runs. It works whether or not the agent implements session/list, and with nothing open it answers without starting an agent.

A session runs one turn at a time. A request for a session that is still running an earlier turn gets a 409 at once, rather than waiting for it: waiting would hold a thread on the scheduler that also answers every running agent's permission and workspace requests, so one caller sending overlapping requests could stall everyone else's. Wait for the earlier turn's response, then send the next.

docs.title: When a turn does not finish
docs.text:
Response Meaning 502 The turn failed or timed out. The response never repeats what the agent said; on /prompt, its requestId finds the details in the logs. 409 The named session is still running an earlier turn. Send the next turn once that one has answered. A turn that timed out keeps its session until the agent has stopped, normally a few milliseconds after the 502 and at most 5 seconds, so a request sent the instant a 502 arrives can meet this. 503 The agent is fine but cannot take another session right now. Try again later. See spring.ai.acp.harness.pool. 200, then an aborted connection /stream only: the turn failed after text was already sent. A stream that ends normally finished its turn.

On OpenCode, each process serves one user at a time, so spring.ai.acp.harness.pool.max-processes limits how many users can hold sessions at once, and a user beyond that gets a 503; see Processes, users and memory.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
With Micrometer on the classpath, every turn and every tool call is an observation: a timer, and a span parented to whatever the caller was in.

spring.ai.acp.harness.turn{spring.ai.kind=acp_harness_turn, spring.ai.acp.harness.runtime=goose, gen_ai.response.model=gpt-5.6-terra, spring.ai.acp.harness.session.kind=named, spring.ai.acp.harness.outcome=END_TURN}
spring.ai.acp.harness.tool.call{spring.ai.kind=acp_harness_tool_call, spring.ai.acp.harness.runtime=goose, spring.ai.acp.harness.tool.kind=READ, spring.ai.acp.harness.tool.status=COMPLETED}

The names follow Spring AI's rule: an OpenTelemetry GenAI key where one means the same thing, and otherwise a key scoped under the observation's own name. So spring.ai.kind is the tag Spring AI puts on its chat client, advisor, tool call and vector store observations, and gen_ai.response.model the key its chat models tag the model with; a breakdown by kind or by model covers the harness beside them. Everything else is spring.ai.acp.harness.*, matching the configuration properties.

gen_ai.response.model is the model the session is really using, not the one requested, and none when the agent kept its own default and never said which, as Spring AI spells an absent value on that key. The outcome is the agent's stop reason, or the exception's simple name when the turn did not reach one; it stays a spring.ai.acp.harness.outcome tag rather than gen_ai.response.finish_reasons, which Spring AI records as a high-cardinality list on the span. Session names, tool titles, context usage and cost are span attributes, not meter tags; contribute an ObservationConvention to change that. Disable with spring.ai.acp.harness.observations.enabled=false.

Observation Low-cardinality tags (meter dimensions) High-cardinality (span attributes) spring.ai.acp.harness.turn spring.ai.kind, spring.ai.acp.harness.runtime, gen_ai.response.model, spring.ai.acp.harness.session.kind, spring.ai.acp.harness.outcome spring.ai.acp.harness.session.name, .context.used, .context.size, .cost spring.ai.acp.harness.tool.call spring.ai.kind, spring.ai.acp.harness.runtime, spring.ai.acp.harness.tool.kind, spring.ai.acp.harness.tool.status spring.ai.acp.harness.tool.title, spring.ai.acp.harness.tool.id

The ACP specification defines no telemetry of its own. It does reserve traceparent, tracestate and baggage inside _meta for W3C trace context, which this client does not yet send.

docs.title: Spring AI ChatModel
docs.text:
Add spring-ai-acp-harness-client-chatmodel and an AcpChatModel bean appears wherever a Spring AI application looks for a ChatModel:

ChatClient chat = ChatClient.create(chatModel);

String answer = chat.prompt()
        .user("Review the pending changes")
        .options(AcpChatOptions.builder().session("review-123").mode("plan").build())
        .call()
        .content();
  • No session (the default): each call is a throwaway ACP session, and the whole message list is sent. Use this with Spring AI's ChatMemory.
  • A named session: the agent already holds the conversation, so only messages after the last assistant message are sent. Don't combine it with a ChatMemory advisor.
  • temperature, topP, maxTokens and similar have no ACP equivalent; they are logged once and ignored. Spring AI ToolCallbacks are not visible to the agent; give it tools as MCP servers.
  • Disable with spring.ai.acp.harness.chat-model.enabled=false.

docs.title: ACP Agent Harness Runtimes
docs.text:
A runtime is an adapter that knows how to launch one agent and what that agent calls its options. Application code never names one; spring.ai.acp.harness.runtime does.

spring.ai.acp.harness.runtime Starter Launches Transport goose spring-ai-acp-harness-client-boot-starter-goose goose acp, or a supervised goose serve stdio, or WebSocket codex spring-ai-acp-harness-client-boot-starter-codex npx -y @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp@2.5.0 stdio opencode spring-ai-acp-harness-client-boot-starter-opencode opencode acp stdio any registry id, e.g. gemini spring-ai-acp-harness-client-boot-starter-registry whatever the ACP registry publishes stdio

docs.title: How the runtime is selected
docs.text:
• One adapter on the classpath: spring.ai.acp.harness.runtime may be left out.
  • Several adapters, or only the registry: it must be set. There is no default agent; startup fails with a message listing the choices.
  • A compiled adapter always wins over the registry for the same id, because it knows things the catalogue does not.
  • A spring.ai.acp.harness.runtimes.<id> block for an id nothing can supply fails startup rather than being silently ignored.

docs.title: Swapping the runtime
docs.text: There are three ways to move an application from one agent to another. None involves changing Java code.

docs.title: 1. Replace the starter
docs.text: Swap spring-ai-acp-harness-client-boot-starter-goose for spring-ai-acp-harness-client-boot-starter-opencode (say), and change or remove spring.ai.acp.harness.runtime. Best when a deployment only ever uses one agent: the other adapters stay off the classpath.

docs.title: 2. Ship several adapters and choose at run time
docs.text:
Put every starter you want to support on the classpath and pick one with any Spring property source:

# command line
java -jar app.jar --spring.ai.acp.harness.runtime=opencode

# environment variable (relaxed binding)
SPRING_AI_ACP_HARNESS_RUNTIME=codex java -jar app.jar

# a profile that carries the runtime and everything that goes with it
java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=codex

A profile is the right tool when the runtimes need different models or credentials, as in the acp-meridian example:

application.yaml
spring:
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        runtime: goose
        model: deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731
        provider: { id: openai, api-type: openai, base-url: ${GENAI_API_BASE}, api-key: ${GENAI_API_KEY} }
---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: codex
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        runtime: codex
        model: gpt-5.6-terra
        provider: { id: openai, api-type: openai, base-url: "", api-key: ${OPENAI_API_KEY} }

docs.title: 3. Let an operator decide with agents.yaml
docs.text:
Import a standalone file with the acp: prefix, and its keys are implicitly under spring.ai.acp.harness. It gets relaxed binding, profiles and ${…} placeholders like any other config file, and validation errors point at its lines. The file may have any name; the prefix, not the name, is what routes it here, so a file another library reads is never taken from it:

application.yaml
spring:
  config:
    import: optional:acp:agents.yaml      # or optional:acp:/etc/myapp/agent-config.yaml
agents.yaml (next to the jar)
runtime: opencode
model: gpt-5.4-mini
permissions:
  policy: deny
runtimes:
  opencode:
    config: { share: disabled }

Keys that already start with spring. are left alone, so the file may carry an unrelated property too.

docs.title: What moves when you swap
docs.text:
Most configuration is portable and carries over unchanged. These are the exceptions worth checking:

Area Portable? What to check MCP servers, skills, workspace, timeout, permissions policy Yes Nothing. AGENTS.md Goose, Codex, OpenCode Registry agents may read another file name (Gemini CLI reads GEMINI.md). See Agent Instructions. spring.ai.acp.harness.model Yes Spelling differences (gpt-5.4-mini vs openai/gpt-5.4-mini) are matched for you, but each agent only offers the models its provider sells. spring.ai.acp.harness.mode Values differ Goose says approve where Codex and OpenCode say plan. See Mode. Own endpoint (provider.base-url) Mostly Codex speaks only the OpenAI Responses API; an endpoint serving only /chat/completions works with Goose and OpenCode but not Codex. spring.ai.acp.harness.runtimes.<id> By design, no Inert for every other runtime, so blocks for several runtimes can stay side by side. Stored session operations Partly Guard with sessions().supports(…). MCP load-failure notices Goose only Other agents do not report an MCP server they failed to load.

docs.title: Installing each agent
docs.text:
Runtime What must be on the machine Pointing at a specific binary goose The goose CLI GOOSE_CLI_PATH environment variable codex Node.js with npx (codex-acp is downloaded on first start) CODEX_ACP_CLI_PATH, or spring.ai.acp.harness.runtimes.codex.command opencode The OpenCode CLI OPENCODE_CLI_PATH, or spring.ai.acp.harness.runtimes.opencode.command registry Nothing; npx or uvx for agents distributed through npm or PyPI Downloaded into spring.ai.acp.harness.registry.cache

A path set with GOOSE_CLI_PATH or OPENCODE_CLI_PATH is checked at startup, so a wrong value fails with a message naming the file. Everything else an agent can be told is covered in Runtime Configuration.

docs.title: Codex
docs.text:
Codex has no ACP mode in its own binary. The adapter runs the @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp npm package, which wraps Codex, and the first start pays an npx download.

application.yaml: every Codex key
spring:
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        runtimes:
          codex:
            package: "@agentclientprotocol/codex-acp@2.5.0"   # what npx runs (this is the default)
            # command: /usr/local/bin/codex-acp                # a pre-installed adapter instead of npx
            args: [ ]                                           # extra arguments for the adapter
            home: /var/lib/codex                                # CODEX_HOME; see "Codex's home directory"
            config-toml:                                        # written as CODEX_HOME/config.toml
              model_reasoning_effort: high
            env:
              RUST_LOG: warn

docs.title: Sandbox and approvals
docs.text:
codex-acp exposes Codex's approval and sandbox settings as three presets of its mode option, and spring.ai.acp.harness.mode selects one:

spring.ai.acp.harness.mode codex-acp name Behaviour read-only Ask for approval Always asks to edit files outside the workspace and to use the internet. Still writes inside the workspace without asking. agent (default) Approve for me Sandboxed; asks only for actions it detects as potentially unsafe. agent-full-access Full access No sandbox: unrestricted access to the internet and to any file the process can reach. Never asks. plan Plan (collaboration_mode) Plans before changing anything; the mode to pair with permissions.policy: deny for a reviewer.

To run Codex outside its sandbox, select full access:

spring:
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        runtime: codex
        mode: agent-full-access
        on-unsupported: fail        # refuse to run if the preset cannot be applied

or only for the turns that need it:

acpHarnessClient.prompt().session("migration").user("Run the full integration build")
        .options(o -> o.mode("agent-full-access"))
        .call();

Important

Setting sandbox_mode or approval_policy in config-toml does not change this. Measured against codex-acp 1.13.0: with sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access" and approval_policy = "never" in config.toml, new sessions still start in agent. Use spring.ai.acp.harness.mode. With on-unsupported: fail you will know if it was not applied.

Warning

Under agent-full-access Codex asks nothing, so spring.ai.acp.harness.permissions never gets a request to refuse. Whatever the JVM's user can reach, the agent can change, and the model's credentials are in its environment. Only run it where the machine or container is itself the sandbox: a disposable container with no secrets beyond the ones it needs, and nothing mounted that you would mind losing.

spring.ai.acp.harness.mode takes one value. codex-acp offers both a mode and a collaboration_mode option, and Spring AI ACP Harness Client applies the value to whichever option offers it.

docs.title: config.toml
docs.text:
config-toml is written as Codex's config.toml. YAML maps become TOML tables, and lists of scalars become arrays. Keys are Codex's own; see the Codex configuration reference.

spring:
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        runtimes:
          codex:
            config-toml:
              model_reasoning_effort: high           # low | medium | high | xhigh | max | ultra, as codex-acp advertises
              model_reasoning_summary: concise
              shell_environment_policy:              # becomes the [shell_environment_policy] table
                inherit: core

model_reasoning_effort is the way to set reasoning effort: codex-acp advertises it as a reasoning_effort option with no portable property, and a value in config.toml becomes that option's starting value (verified against 1.13.0).

Caution

The file the adapter writes is the only config.toml Codex reads. Setting config-toml moves CODEX_HOME to a directory the adapter owns, so a developer's ~/.codex/config.toml (their model, MCP servers, profiles) stops applying. That is deliberate, since a server should not depend on a personal file, but it can surprise you locally.

docs.title: Codex's home directory and credentials
docs.text:
Codex keeps its config and its login (auth.json) under CODEX_HOME, so where that points decides both:

Configuration CODEX_HOME Credentials used No config-toml, no key, no endpoint Inherited (~/.codex) The existing codex login, untouched config-toml only <runtime-home> The existing login, linked in (a symlink to ~/.codex/auth.json) spring.ai.acp.harness.provider.api-key against OpenAI <runtime-home> That key, sent with ACP authenticate and held in memory only A bring-your-own endpoint <runtime-home> The endpoint's key, read by Codex from the environment home set That directory As above, but in the directory you chose

Warning

Do not point home at your own ~/.codex while also setting config-toml or a provider: the adapter writes config.toml into its home and would replace yours.

docs.title: Pinning or pre-installing codex-acp
docs.text: package pins the npm version npx runs; the default is the version this release was tested against. To avoid the download at startup, for example in a container image, install the adapter at build time and set command to it. package is then ignored, and args are passed to the command you named.

docs.title: Runtime Configuration
docs.text:
Each agent has settings of its own that ACP does not standardize: Goose's built-in extensions, Codex's sandbox, OpenCode's per-tool permissions. They live in the third configuration tier, one block per runtime:

application.yaml
spring:
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        runtime: goose
        runtimes:
          goose:    { builtins: developer }                       # used: goose is selected
          codex:    { config-toml: { model_reasoning_effort: high } }   # ignored until codex is selected
          opencode: { config: { share: disabled } }               # ignored until opencode is selected

  • Only the selected runtime reads its block. Blocks for the others are inert, so an application can keep settings for every agent it supports side by side. A block for an id that no adapter or registry can supply fails startup, which catches a misspelled runtime name.

  • Applied last. Whatever the adapter derives from portable properties (provider credentials, a bring-your-own endpoint) is written first, and the tier-3 block is laid over it. env therefore wins over every variable the adapter sets. For the config-file blocks the merge is by top-level key, so a top-level key you set replaces the adapter's value for that key, including a whole table.

  • Any property source works. Top-level keys bind relaxed, while nested keys keep the spelling you wrote, because they end up verbatim in a file the agent parses:

    spring.ai.acp.harness.runtimes.codex.config-toml.model_reasoning_effort=high
spring.ai.acp.harness.runtimes.goose.env.GOOSE_MAX_TURNS=40

  • Files are written to spring.ai.acp.harness.runtime-home (a directory under the JVM's temp directory by default), never to the workspace.

Tip

Prefer the portable property whenever one exists. It keeps working when you swap agents, and the negotiated ones report what was applied. Use tier 3 for what is genuinely agent-specific.

To set… Use Not Model, mode, provider spring.ai.acp.harness.model, .mode, .provider GOOSE_MODEL, GOOSE_MODE, model in config-toml or config MCP servers spring.ai.acp.harness.mcp-servers Goose extensions, Codex mcp_servers, OpenCode mcp Skills spring.ai.acp.harness.skills OpenCode skills paths Instructions <workspace>/AGENTS.md OpenCode instructions, unless you need more than one file

docs.title: Goose
docs.text:
The adapter launches goose acp over stdio and sets GOOSE_DISABLE_KEYRING=1 and GOOSE_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false. Goose still reads its own ~/.config/goose/config.yaml for anything not set here, including which of its built-in extensions are on.

application.yaml: every Goose key
spring:
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        runtimes:
          goose:
            builtins: [ developer, todo, skills ]  # --with-builtin; a comma-separated string works too
            env:                                   # environment for the goose process, applied last
              GOOSE_THINKING_EFFORT: high
              GOOSE_MAX_TURNS: "40"
            serve:                                 # speak ACP over goose's WebSocket server instead of stdio
              transport: websocket                 # stdio (default) | websocket
              host: 127.0.0.1
              port: 0                              # 0 = any free port
              startup-timeout: PT30S
            log-dir: /var/log/goose/logs           # where goose writes its log, if not the default
            mcp:
              answer-discover: true                # workaround for MCP gateways; see below

docs.title: Built-in extensions
docs.text:
Goose's own tools come from extensions bundled in the binary. A session gets two sets of them:

  1. Goose's defaults, as its config.yaml enables them. With no config.yaml, which is usual on a server or in a container, goose enables the defaults listed below. They load alongside the servers in spring.ai.acp.harness.mcp-servers, not instead of them.
  2. Whatever builtins names, each passed as --with-builtin. These are added to the first set.

So builtins can only add extensions. Leaving developer out of it does not take the shell away from the agent; see Turning a goose default off.

Goose 1.52's extensions, by the name builtins takes:

Name On by default Provides developer Yes shell, write, edit, tree and read_image: commands and file changes in the workspace. Needed to run a skill's scripts. analyze Yes Code structure through tree-sitter: directory overviews, file details, call graphs. apps Yes Tools to create and manage goose "apps" (HTML/CSS/JavaScript run in a sandboxed window). extensionmanager Yes Tools to search for, enable and disable further extensions during a session. summon Yes load and delegate: load knowledge, and hand tasks to subagents. skills Yes load_skill: Agent Skills from the workspace's .agents/skills. tom Yes "Top of mind": adds the text in GOOSE_MOIM_MESSAGE_TEXT or GOOSE_MOIM_MESSAGE_FILE to every turn. No tools. scheduler Yes, but not loaded Scheduled recipe runs. Goose loads it only under goose acp --enable-scheduler, which the adapter does not pass. todo No A task list the agent keeps for multi-step work. Reported as the agent's plan (PlanUpdated); see below. chatrecall No Searching past conversations and loading their summaries. summarize No Loading files or directories and returning an LLM summary in one call. code_execution No "Code mode": the agent calls other extensions by writing code, to save tokens. orchestrator No Managing other goose sessions: list, start, message, interrupt and stop them. computercontroller No Web scraping, file caching and automation. Runs as a bundled MCP server. memory No Tools to save and retrieve durable memories. Runs as a bundled MCP server. autovisualiser No Data visualisation and UI generation (charts, diagrams). Runs as a bundled MCP server. tutorial No Interactive goose tutorials. Rarely useful in an application.

The list and the defaults change between goose releases. todo was on by default in goose 1.45 and is off in 1.52, for example. To see what your goose enables, run goose info -v with the same environment the application gives it: it prints the effective extensions section, defaults included.

application.yaml: add the task list to goose's defaults
spring:
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        runtimes:
          goose:
            builtins: todo                 # or a list: [ todo, memory ]

Warning

Because of the defaults, an agent on goose has a shell and file tools unless something turns them off. Under spring.ai.acp.harness.mode: auto or an auto-approve permission policy it uses them without asking, and the shell inherits your application's environment, secrets included. spring.ai.acp.harness.filesystem and spring.ai.acp.harness.terminal do not govern it: those lend the client's disk and terminal, and this shell is the agent's own.

docs.title: The todo list as the agent's plan
docs.text:
Goose sends no ACP plan updates. Its task list is the todo extension, and each change to it is an ordinary tool call, todo__todo_write, carrying the whole list as markdown. The adapter reads that call as the plan: it arrives as AcpHarnessEvent.PlanUpdated, and neither the call nor its update is reported as a tool call. A UI that renders the plan for Codex or OpenCode renders goose's task list the same way.

  • - [x] is completed, - [ ] is pending, and - [-], - [~], - [/] or - [>] is in progress. Goose's own template uses only the first two, so a list usually shows items done and not yet done, rarely one in progress.
  • A status word is read wherever a model tends to put it: trailing ("Draft report — in progress", "… (done)", "… [DONE]") or leading ("[DONE] Draft report"). It is dropped from the entry's text. A ✅, ✔ or ☑ in front of an item, or strikethrough, means completed. Anything else is pending. Models do not always follow goose's template.
  • Sub-items become entries of their own, since ACP's plan is flat. Headings and prose lines are skipped.
  • A write with no list items in it is reported as the tool call it is. An empty write clears the plan.

The agent writes a list only when it decides to, so name the tool in AGENTS.md or the prompt when you want one: "Keep a todo list with one item per request you draft."

docs.title: Turning a goose default off
docs.text:
Goose reads which defaults to enable from its config.yaml, and an entry with enabled: false takes one away. Nothing else needs to be in the file:

config.yaml: no shell, no extension manager
extensions:
  developer:
    enabled: false
  extensionmanager:
    enabled: false

The adapter does not move goose's configuration, so goose looks for this file in its usual place: ~/.config/goose/config.yaml for the user the application runs as. On a developer machine that is your own goose configuration. To give the application a file of its own, point GOOSE_PATH_ROOT at a directory through the env block. Goose then reads <root>/config/config.yaml, and keeps its sessions and logs under that root too, so set log-dir to <root>/state/logs as well (see below). A name disabled in the file and also listed in builtins is loaded: builtins wins.

Note

A misspelled name does not stop goose. It writes Failed to load extension <name>: … Unknown extension (since 1.55.0, failed to start extension with the name and Unknown extension in fields of their own) to its log and carries on. Spring AI ACP Harness Client (SAAHC) reads that log for agents it started, so the mistake appears as a WARN line and in AcpHarnessClient.notices(), worded as a server that could not be loaded.

For tools that are not built in, declare an MCP server under spring.ai.acp.harness.mcp-servers rather than a goose extension. It is the same thing to goose, and it stays portable.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Goose reads each of its config.yaml settings from an environment variable of the same name first, so the env block can set any of them. Some that are useful from an application:

Variable Effect GOOSE_THINKING_EFFORT Reasoning effort: off, low, medium, high, max. Goose advertises this as its thinking_effort option, which has no portable property. GOOSE_MAX_TURNS Maximum agent turns without user input. GOOSE_AUTO_COMPACT_THRESHOLD, GOOSE_CONTEXT_LIMIT When goose compacts its context, and the context size it assumes. GOOSE_TEMPERATURE Sampling temperature, for providers that accept one. OPENAI_BASE_PATH Pins the OpenAI wire API (e.g. v1/chat/completions). Left unset, goose chooses per model; see Bring your own endpoint. GOOSE_DISABLE_KEYRING "0" lets goose read secrets from the OS keychain again (the adapter disables it for servers).

Environment values are strings, so quote numbers in YAML. GOOSE_MODE, GOOSE_PROVIDER and GOOSE_MODEL work too, but use the portable spring.ai.acp.harness.mode, .provider and .model instead.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
spring.ai.acp.harness.mode Behaviour auto (default) Edits, creates and deletes files and uses extensions freely. No permission requests. approve Every tool call, extension use and file change asks first. smart_approve Asks before editing, creating or deleting files and using extensions. chat No tools at all: the model only converses.

In approve and smart_approve, each question is answered by spring.ai.acp.harness.permissions.

docs.title: Running goose as a WebSocket server
docs.text: With serve.transport: websocket, the adapter starts goose serve on host and port, generates a secret it sends as a header on every connection, and supervises the process: it is health-checked and restarted with backoff, and stopped when the application closes. Use it when you want goose to outlive individual connections, as the goose buildpack did. Stdio stays the default because it is what every other runtime supports. Keep host on loopback unless you mean to expose the server.

docs.title: Log directory and MCP gateways
docs.text:
• log-dir tells SAAHC where goose writes its log, which is the only place goose reports an MCP server or extension it could not load. Defaults to $XDG_STATE_HOME/goose/logs, else ~/.local/state/goose/logs. Set it only if your deployment moves goose's state.
  • mcp.answer-discover: true answers goose's server/discover probe on behalf of MCP gateways that reply to it with an error goose cannot correlate. See MCP Servers.

docs.title: OpenCode
docs.text:
The adapter launches opencode acp over stdio. OpenCode advertises exactly two options, model and mode, so nearly all of its behaviour is configured through its own opencode.json.

application.yaml: every OpenCode key
spring:
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        runtimes:
          opencode:
            command: /opt/opencode/bin/opencode   # default: OPENCODE_CLI_PATH, else "opencode" on the PATH
            args: [ --print-logs ]
            config:                               # written as opencode.json, pointed at by OPENCODE_CONFIG
              share: disabled
              autoupdate: false
            config-file: /etc/myapp/opencode.json # where to write it, instead of <runtime-home>/opencode.json
            env:
              HTTPS_PROXY: http://proxy.internal:3128

docs.title: opencode.json
docs.text:
config is written as JSON with OpenCode's own keys; see the OpenCode config reference. OpenCode merges configuration files rather than replacing them, in this order (later wins, key by key):

  1. the global ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json;
  2. the file the adapter writes (OPENCODE_CONFIG);
  3. a project opencode.json in the workspace.

Measured against opencode 1.18.31: a model in the workspace's opencode.json overrode the one in the adapter's file, while the adapter's other keys still applied. Unlike Codex, relocating the config file does not affect OpenCode's login, which lives elsewhere.

docs.title: Per-tool permissions
docs.text:
OpenCode's permission block sets, per tool, whether it may act (allow), must not (deny), or must ask (ask). An ask reaches your application as an ACP permission request and is answered by spring.ai.acp.harness.permissions. This gives you a review gate in the default build mode, finer than switching to plan:

spring:
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        runtimes:
          opencode:
            config:
              permission:
                edit: ask                  # every file change asks
                bash:
                  "*": ask                 # shell commands ask…
                  "git status": allow      # …except these
                  "git diff*": allow
                webfetch: deny
                external_directory: deny   # nothing outside the workspace
        permissions:
          policy: deny                     # every ask is refused: the agent reads, and runs only git status/diff

Tools include read, edit, glob, grep, list, bash, task, webfetch, websearch, skill and external_directory. A single value (permission: ask) applies to all of them.

docs.title: Modes and custom agents
docs.text:
OpenCode's modes are its primary agents: build (the default) and plan. Define your own in config.agent and it becomes a mode that spring.ai.acp.harness.mode can select. Verified against 1.18.31, where a custom review agent appeared as a mode beside build and plan and could be set:

spring:
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        runtime: opencode
        mode: review                        # select the agent defined below
        runtimes:
          opencode:
            config:
              agent:
                review:
                  mode: primary             # primary agents are ACP modes
                  description: Reviews changes without editing them
                  prompt: You review code for correctness and security. Never edit files.
                  permission:
                    edit: deny
                    bash: ask

default_agent in config sets the mode new sessions start in. Prefer spring.ai.acp.harness.mode, which reports whether it was applied.

docs.title: Processes, users and memory
docs.text:
OpenCode keeps MCP clients per process rather than per session. It holds one client per server name, and every session/new replaces it, so all the sessions in a process call MCP through whichever session declared the servers last (see Credentials the agent never sees). To keep one user's tools from running with another user's credentials, the pool gives each OpenCode process to one principal at a time:

  • A user's sessions all share one process, up to spring.ai.acp.harness.pool.max-sessions-per-process.
  • A user who needs a process gets an idle one. An idle process that last served someone else is restarted first, which takes a second or two and does not count against max-restarts.
  • When every process is serving other users, a new user's session is refused with an error that names spring.ai.acp.harness.pool.max-processes. A process becomes free when its user's last session closes, either explicitly or after spring.ai.acp.harness.pool.session-ttl of inactivity.

So max-processes is the number of users who can hold OpenCode sessions at the same time, and each of them costs a whole OpenCode process. Processes start lazily, so memory grows with concurrent users rather than being allocated at startup. The goose and Codex adapters keep MCP servers per session, so for them max-processes is only about parallelism.

Measured resident memory of one opencode acp process:

Point Linux x86_64, 1.18.33 macOS arm64, 1.18.32 After initialize 490 MB 420 MB After the first session/new 430 MB 550 MB After a first short turn not measured 660 MB Each further session in the same process not measured about 1 MB

Budget about 650 MB per OpenCode process, plus your application's own JVM. Size the host or container for the worst case:

memory ≥ JVM + max-processes × 650 MB
application.yaml: up to three concurrent users
spring:
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        runtime: opencode
        pool:
          max-processes: 3             # 3 users, ~2 GB of OpenCode
          max-sessions-per-process: 8  # chats per user
          session-ttl: 30m             # free idle users sooner

Note

The agent processes are children of the JVM and share its memory limit. On Cloud Foundry, the Java buildpack's memory calculator gives the JVM nearly the whole container by default, so leave room for OpenCode with memory_calculator: { headroom: … } in JBP_CONFIG_OPEN_JDK_JRE (a percentage of the container), or cap the heap with -Xmx in JAVA_OPTS. Otherwise the container can be killed for exceeding its limit while the JVM still believes it has headroom.

docs.title: Other useful settings
docs.text:
Key under config Effect share: disabled Never publish sessions to OpenCode's share service. Recommended for servers. autoupdate: false Do not update the binary at run time; pin the version in your image instead. small_model A cheaper provider/model for side tasks such as session titles. instructions Extra instruction files or globs, loaded as well as AGENTS.md. enabled_providers, disabled_providers Restrict which of OpenCode's built-in providers can be used. snapshot: false Stop recording filesystem snapshots for undo, which saves disk in large workspaces.

Note

With a bring-your-own endpoint, the adapter writes provider, model and disabled_providers into the same file. A top-level key of the same name in config replaces the adapter's value outright, so leave those three to spring.ai.acp.harness.provider unless you intend to describe the providers yourself.

docs.title: Registry agents
docs.text:
With spring-ai-acp-harness-client-boot-starter-registry, spring.ai.acp.harness.runtime can name any agent in the ACP registry that no compiled adapter claims. The agent is resolved from a cached catalogue snapshot, downloaded, verified against its published SHA-256, unpacked and launched:

spring:
  ai:
    acp:
      harness:
        runtime: gemini
        registry:
          require-checksum: true        # default; refuse agents published without a sha256
          cache: ${user.home}/.spring-ai-acp/agents
          refresh: 24h
          offline: false                # true: bundled snapshot and already-installed agents only
        runtimes:
          gemini:
            args: [ --debug ]           # appended to the arguments the registry specifies
            env:
              GEMINI_API_KEY: ${GEMINI_API_KEY}

A registry agent has only two tier-3 keys, args and env, because nothing is known about its config files. It reaches the negotiated tier only through ACP's own option categories and the obvious ids model, mode and provider. Provider credentials reach it as <API_TYPE>_API_KEY and <API_TYPE>_BASE_URL; anything else goes in env.

Warning

A registry agent is an executable downloaded from the internet and run with your application's credentials in its environment. Several binary agents publish no checksum; running one requires spring.ai.acp.harness.registry.require-checksum: false, which you should set only deliberately. Pin the catalogue with a file: URL in spring.ai.acp.harness.registry.url for reproducible builds.
